concern_details.detail: What are the main components involved in the seat booking functionality?
concern_details.why: The view shows the three entry points, the facade, the reservation, room and notification managers, the seat assignment strategy, the model, the registries and persistence. These match the booking path in the code: ReservationController and ReservationSummary call LibraryFacade.makeReservation, which calls ReservationManager.makeReservation, which uses Area, Seat, Student, the registries and the strategy. It leaves out the booking request/response DTOs (ReservationRequestDTO, ReservationDTO). They are the data that enters every booking from both entry points.

concern_details.detail: What is each of these components responsible for?
concern_details.why: The diagram shows only names. All the responsibilities are in inventory.json, which the stakeholder does not see in the picture. Most of all, the diagram does not show where the existing booking rules live. ReservationManager.makeReservation runs the flow (resolve room/area/slot, validateSeatInArea, validateUniqueness, availableSeats, selectSeat, createAndSave). The rule predicates themselves are in the model (Seat.isAvailable, Area.getAvailableSeats, Student.hasActiveOrConfirmedReservationForDateAndSlot, StudyRoom.isOpenOnDate) and in ReservationRegistry.occupiesSlot. A developer adding a booking rule needs exactly this.

concern_details.detail: How do these components interact with each other?
concern_details.why: The labelled dependencies follow the call chain, and the spot checks agree with the code: the facade delegates to ReservationManager and NotificationManager.sendReminders, the scheduler calls manageReservationEnd and sendReminders through the facade, entity Seat/Student/Area call ReservationRegistry/StudyRoomRegistry, and NotificationManager updates through ReservationRegistry. Two things are not visible. The resMgr-to-notifMgr notification goes through the Observer on Reservation (reservation.attach(NotificationManager)). The order of steps inside the booking flow is also not shown, which is acceptable for a package view.

concern_details.detail: Which parts of the system may be affected by modifying the seat booking functionality?
concern_details.why: The blue/plain/grey classes are a reasonable way to show impact. Two problems weaken them. First, the impact classification is only a hidden styling stereotype and a colour legend, with no reason given per element. Second, it leaves out impacts the code shows: the request DTO and both entry UIs change when a rule needs new input, and Room availability manager shows availability using the same model/registry predicates (Seat.isAvailable, occupiesSlot), so a rule that changes availability changes what it shows. That makes it 'likely affected', not just 'may be affected', and the omitted roomMgr-to-model dependency is the link that shows it.

level_why: For a balanced level, about ten packages in three groups without classes is appropriate. Nothing needs to be cut. The fixes below add short responsibility text and one or two dependencies, not new class-level elements, so the view stays at the balanced level.
missing: The responsibility of each package in the view itself (for example as a short note or in the package body): the code shows ReservationManager.makeReservation running the validation sequence and the model/registries holding the rule predicates.

Booking request/response DTOs (dto.ReservationRequestDTO, ReservationDTO): used by ReservationController, ReservationSummary, LibraryFacade and ReservationManager, and a likely change point when a new rule needs new input or new error data.

Room availability manager ..> Reservation and seat model (and Seat assignment strategy ..> model): the README admits these were omitted, but the roomMgr dependency is the reason displayed availability is affected by a rule change.
uml: In the rendered diagram the package tab shows the PlantUML alias (swing, resMgr, registries...) as the package name, and the readable name appears as body text. The package name should be the meaningful name, without code aliases.

Several 'packages' are single classes (Library facade = LibraryFacade, Reservation manager = ReservationManager, Reservation scheduler = NotificationScheduler). In a package diagram these could be classes nested in their package (controller, boundary), or the packages should be named after the real Java packages (boundary.Swing, boundary.SpringBoot, controller, controller.strategy, entity, database) with the parts as members.

Non-standard stereotypes <<accent>> and <<muted>> carry the impact meaning. They are hidden, but the change-impact information is then encoded only in colour, not in UML. Use a note or a comment per element instead.
fixes: Show each package's responsibility in the diagram (a short line or a note), and say explicitly that the booking rules are run in ReservationManager.makeReservation and implemented as predicates in the model (Seat.isAvailable, Area.getAvailableSeats, Student.hasActiveOrConfirmedReservationForDateAndSlot, StudyRoom.isOpenOnDate) and in ReservationRegistry.occupiesSlot.

Show the change impact with UML notes or comments that give the reason (for example 'new rule check added here', 'availability shown to users uses the same predicates'), not with colour plus hidden custom stereotypes.
Add a 'Booking DTOs' package (ReservationRequestDTO, ReservationDTO) used by the entry points, the facade and the Reservation manager, and mark it as possibly affected.
Add the Room availability manager ..> Reservation and seat model dependency and move roomMgr to likely affected, because it shows availability using the same predicates.
Make the package names the readable names (not the aliases swing/resMgr/...), and consider aligning the packages with the real Java packages, with single classes as members.
